item.title: Trump DOUBLES DOWN as Iran War DESTROYS the Economy
item.description:
Scott Galloway and Jessica Tarlov talk about the Iran war's growing economic toll. Trump is once again claiming the U.S. will win in Iran — even as he publicly rejected Tehran's recent offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile oil prices have soared to over $100 a barrel, up from $72 in February before the war began. In the bond market, the ten-year Treasury yield is at its highest level in two decades. With Trump now planning to spend the next 30 days campaigning for Republicans in traditionally red states, he'll have to balance political priorities at home with a war that's increasingly hitting Americans in their wallets.
The Trump administration's Education Department has officially rescinded the Biden-era interpretation of Title IX that included protections for sexual orientation and gender identity. Education Secretary Linda McMahon says the move will reduce confusion for parents, students, and educational institutions. Does this actually change much on the ground — or is it primarily about optics for a base that views gender as a defining issue?
A new lawsuit has put the “Cornell Seven” back in the spotlight. A former Cornell student alleges she was drugged and sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members in 2024. Prosecutors initially declined to file charges but have now reopened the investigation and are seeking a grand jury review. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Ortez (D-NY) weighed in publicly. Where does the case go from here?
In Los Angeles, new polling shows in the mayoral race shows Democratic Socialist city councilmember Nithya Raman leading the incumbent mayor Karen Bass by 11 points — a dramatic reversal from the June primary when Bass finished five points ahead of Raman. 63% of likely voters view Bass unfavorably, with majorities panning her response to the Palisades Fire. Raman is dominating among younger voters, and Kalshi currently has her odds of winning at 57%. How did Raman pull off this turnaround — and will the race tighten before November, or will another of America’s largest and most Democratic cities be led by a DSA member?

Transcript

[music] >> Welcome to Rage and Reason. I'm Scott Galloway. >> And I'm Jessica Tarlov. >> Before we get started, we're just 35 days out until the midterms. Make sure to hit subscribe to support our show and help us reach new audiences. All right, let's bust into it. Trump is once again claiming the US will win in the war against Iran, despite publicly rejecting Tehran's recent offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's foreign minister says Tehran still hasn't received a formal answer for the proposal, but expects one today. Meanwhile, Brent crude has reached over

$100 a barrel again, up from $72 in February before the war began. The 10-year Treasury yield is at its highest level in two decades. And with Trump now planning to spend the next 30 days campaigning for Republicans in traditionally red states, he'll have to balance his political priorities at home with a war that's increasingly hitting Americans in the wallet. Let's listen to Mike Johnson talk about the situation this morning. >> The big question is, should Iran have a nuclear weapon? I think every American says they should not. That would be a danger to us and everybody around the world. Every administration for almost 50 years had the same objective to

ensure that didn't happen. They got this close. I'm on the gang of eight. I got the inside highest level classified briefing. It was a very, very dangerous and imminent situation and we had to take care of it. Operation Epic Fury was an epic success. Now we got to resolve that. The president's laser focused on it. You've heard developments over the last 24, 36 hours. I think we're getting very close to that. I think Iran is running out of resources to sell. They're letting out of 15 million barrels of oil to sell to China, we think. Um, and so we're entering a new phase of this. >> He's like half right in that the past 24 to 36 hours have actually looked like

some of what we were doing in the strait has paid off. Um, so reports now and they couldn't actually physically see the tankers that were going through because they were doing it completely, you know, in the pitch dark without lights on, but it looks like and the Wall Street Journal's reporting this as well that 80% of the pre-war levels of regional flow are now out into the system. And so Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz is significantly weakened. You would not at all say at this moment that they were choking it

off. Um, that could have crazy implications in that these are a bunch of lunatics and so maybe they lash out militarily as a response to this. Um, but Iran's currency is enormously weakened. Um, it's just hit an all-time low. Uh, 2,500,000 to 1 US dollar for the rial and gas prices have ticked down a little bit. Um, you know, a few cents here and there. Biggest drops were in the Midwest, somewhere that Republicans need

to do better, um, and in the Gulf Coast uh, for diesel. So, I think we got to say it it's a good thing that this oil is getting out of there and that Iran is in a weakened position, but there is also no evidence that the ultimate goal here and where Mike Johnson led from, which is I think we would all agree that we don't want Iran to have a nuclear weapon. You don't have a bunch of sane people that are coming to the table and I'm not sure that you would even be able to get back to the JCPOA level deal that we had from the

Obama administration. So, weakened and in a worse position, um, than they were a couple of weeks ago. 100% there. Um, but his uh, his glasses are a little too rose-colored, I would say, especially since this guy's also out there saying that the Republicans are going to expand their majority in the house. Like I there is no one that diluted who's saying that. I mean, even the most, you know, pro-Trump or conservative Republicans who think that they've been delivering left, right, and center

understand that they're going to lose the House. The question is, what's the margin going to be? >> Yeah, it it does feel like a lot of happy talk and all this nonsense around, you know, I think Americans are willing to pay a little bit more for you know, for Iran not getting a nuclear weapon. They didn't have a nuclear weapon. I mean, it's just so This is an arsonist showing up to the site where the home is burned down the next day and grabbing a hose and wanting credit for it. It's literally like, okay, we broke it and we want credit for, you know, kind of sort of trying to fix it. In terms of the oil math, Brent

went from $72 to over $100, up 40% since the war started. Rule of thumb, it's about 2 and 1/2 cents a gallon for every dollar, so gas is up, sort of call it 60 cents to a buck, depending on where you are. And that's kind of the Iran war tax that every American pays every week and they get reminded of it. Oil shocks preceded recessions of '73, '79, and 2008. So, oil shocks aren't a leading indicator of a recession, they're a leading cause of it. The 10-year being at a two-decade high is a pretty big deal. It's the market saying it doesn't trust the plan. Higher

yields means 7% mortgages, pricier car loans, more interest on the debt. At the end of the day, that the bond market is the adult in the room that just isn't impressed with Trump and it's kind of it's kind of the only voter that Trump can't primary, if you will. With respect to rejecting Iran's offer from the Iranians around the Strait of Hormuz, yeah, when the IRGC offers to reopen the world's most important oil choke point and you say no, yeah, you bet you need to have a better idea. Having said that, and there is no evidence there is one.

I don't think their offer is sincere. I think they just want to keep poking him enough such that he doesn't do continue to military strikes, but it's clear that they won. The tell here, and I'm curious to to your thoughts, is campaigning in red states. >> Yeah. >> You don't spend the last 30 days defending Texas and Florida if you think you're winning. >> Or Oklahoma and Kansas. >> It's not a victory. They It's a fire drill. They've decided to break glass. The war Wars that don't end become taxes that don't end, and it's clear they are playing defense right now. Thoughts? >> 100% agree with that. And Axios was also

reporting on the war front that apparently Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release of frozen funds for concrete progress on nuclear. Um I can't wait to rehash, quote unquote, pallets of cash uh with some of my colleagues who have been distorting the truth about what happened during the Obama administration. But it is a complete fire drill. I mean, the it's diametrically opposed to what happened in 2024 when I, and I had egg on my face about this, was sitting around saying like, "You know, what are

you doing doing a big rally at Madison Square Garden? Like, why are you campaigning all over California or other blue states, right?" And then I found out why. Because every arrow on that New York Times graphic headed in the red direction except for I think, you know, one suburb outside of Atlanta that was still heading blue. And they expanded the map enormously, right? For people who weren't traditional Republican voters, getting young voters, Latino voters, black voters. Um it is the

opposite what's going on now. They're having to go to like the Rotary Club and beg 70-year-old white people to stick with the Republican Party. And that's a very bad place to be in 35 days out. Um I want to obviously talk more about the electoral stuff and what's going on in specific races, but I am curious what you think about the fact that 80% of the flows that used to come out of the Strait of Hormuz are apparently making it out of there. What do you think that does to the negotiating table and and what Iran

may do vis-a-vis a deal? Do you think now some sort of military [clears throat] activation is more likely that they're going to lash out and that's the way that they can lash out and hurt us. They know about our munition stockpile being severely depleted. They also know that the region has no appetite for any kind of war at this point and that our Gulf allies, you know, wish that they could just close their eyes and go back in time and like that this didn't happen. >> I think that they've effectively gained control of the Strait of Hormuz even if

even if the flow of oil goes through there, I think they've established the ability to close it by just threatening. I mean, there's been very few actual collateral damage, but it's it's not that the ships won't go through. It's that insurance companies won't insure the ships going through. And so long as the region is hostile, I believe that they've effectively set up a toll similar to what the Panama Canal does and that Iran controls it right now. And that they are now in a position that once America sufficiently withdrawn its

military capability from the region, they'll reassert that strength and be able to charge tolls. And they know that the American public has no appetite for continued military involvement. So, there's just no getting around it. I I think we lost on middle power here and they're trying to portray it as some sort of victory and the American public isn't buying it. I just think this is I think we've lost. I don't think the American Trump does not have the support to for further military action. They know that we're we're leaving. It's

like what is it Ho Chi Minh said? We will kill some of theirs, they will kill many of ours, they will tire, they will go home. I mean, that's what he said and he was right. And that's what's happened here. Now, having said that, about the time you think you understand something, there's so many, you know, known unknowns or unknown unknowns. The Iranian economy is in shambles right now. You know, you know, it's hard to understand the atmospherics that led to so many protests back, you know, >> Yeah, January.

>> Yeah, that could potentially happen again. So, I was like to ask myself, what could go right? Uh, you could see, I mean, Assad looked impenetrable until he wasn't, right? So, you know, we could It feels as if we're in for or are due for what I'd call a good surprise, but the fact pattern here is the following or the line, the data on the line is that a middle power has stuck up the middle finger and endured tremendous collateral damage, but has essentially repelled, you know,

in their eyes and to their people, the kind of evil empire that is America and and Israel, and has established itself as I don't call it the superpower in the region, but is but has repelled the United States. This is a loss. This is an L for America. Would you argue it's a win for the IRGC? Probably, although I got to think their relationships with their neighbors are hugely strained and it's an enormous loss, I think, over the medium term for America and its Gulf allies. At the

bottom line is the Gulf allies just no longer trust the US and the US had a very strong relationship with many of the Gulf powers. And I think that's going to take a long time uh, to repair, but I don't see any reason I think the sweet spot for Iranian uh, IRGC's approach to this is to poke the bear enough to make it clear that they have not agreed to anything, that they are not by any means feel pressured to comply with American demands, but at the same time not enough such that they would warrant a support for or legitimacy for more military

strikes, which in that bar keeps getting higher and higher because America just really does like the idea when you have Mike Rogers saying we need to get out of Iran in the midst of an election >> met a war he didn't like. >> Yeah, saying we need to get out, we need to leave now, it means there's really a total lack of support. Any thoughts? >> Yeah, well, they also know the Iranians that we're only going to go up to a certain point and that we'll then probably say to the brave Iranian people, you know, make your voices heard again, take to the streets, but the

Iranians are wise enough to remember what happened last time. When they did take to the streets, 50,000 of them were murdered and President Trump said, "Don't worry, help is on the way." And lo and behold, nada came. So, I imagine that we are not going to see a redux of that even as the economy continues to tumble like this and people are living in abject poverty. But there's no reason to for them to think that they're going to be getting any US support and they see the writing on the wall, fact that, you know, there

is a big election coming up that is pivotal for them and Trump has been teasing, you know, a deal is coming after it's like the $5,000, right? Like if you if you stick with me, like things are going to get good. I'm going to put money in your pocket and I'm going to have the most beautiful deal with Iran and, you know, no one is buying any of this. Um, so, in general, I agree with you. I was just really curious about your your take on all of that oil getting out because I was surprised to see that and I think a lot of analysts were not expecting that that much was getting through under the cover of

darkness. >> Yeah, I I listened to um the Secretary of Energy recently and it's not back to where it was, but it oil is flowing. The silver lining in all of this is you got to think that every government around the world that isn't a net oil exporter really feels a strategic imperative to invest in renewables. It's just because not only is it is there economic incentive, but defense incentive. I mean, South Korea's economy and Taiwan's economy, it gets shut down if for whatever reason

they can't produce enough of their own energy. Now, the gray and the silver of the silver lining is that the big winner is China who manufactures the vast majority of renewables, solar panels, batteries, EVs. So, this is a huge, in my opinion, transition in power from from uh the West to China, but also, I believe in potentially 5 years, you're going to see sub 40 or $30 oil. I just got to think so much money as new found capital is going to go into renewables that the the pressure on um

fossil fuels will continue to go down. Uh I mean, I had Timothy Snyder on yesterday and he said something really interesting. He said that if we'd taken a fraction of the money we'd spent on these wars in the Gulf the last 30 years to expedite the transition from fossil fuels to renewables, we wouldn't have needed to be in any of these wars and many of the nation-states or rogue nations would not have the funding to wreak the havoc they wreak. That we could have an inspired this upward spiral of prosperity and a lack of war if we had taken the money we spent on war and spent it on, again, escalating or speeding up the transition to

renewables. I thought that was a very interesting take, but China comes out of this a big winner. Also, again, I I to think that renewables are going to are going to boom here. >> Well, that would be nice. >> Support for the show comes from Gruns. Meanwhile, at home, Trump's Education Department has officially rescinded the Biden era interpretation of Title IX that included protections for sexual orientation and gender identity. Education Secretary Linda McMahon says the move will reduce confusion for parents, students, and educational

institutions. Jess, does this actually change much or is it just about optics, knowing gender is such a hot-button issue for Republicans in particular? >> Uh both. It does change much and it is a hot-button issue and they can't run on the economy, so they're going to run on cruelty. Um the cruelty is the point. It has always been the point here. Um this statement from Linda McMahon, I just what an incredible load of crap. We will continue to relentlessly champion equal opportunity for all Americans and hold accountable any school or college that violates the rights, privacy, or

athletic opportunities for our women and girls. Equal opportunity for all Americans. When have you heard that used to describe what's going on in the Trump administration? Or when have they been decent or respected the First Amendment vis-à-vis what goes on on our universities? I mean, they've had to be slapped back after court after court but this is their vendetta against higher education and wokeism and liberalism, whatever you want to call it. You know, these are

people who when they say equal opportunity for all, I just completely glaze over here. And I do think it's interesting, you know, Linda McMahon is one of those cabinet secretaries we rarely hear from. Right, like she sits in those meetings but she doesn't even do the dear leader stuff really. She's kind of like in the corner, you know, waiting I guess for her big moment where she can come out with, you know, something that is so rooted in hurting people. And this is coming from someone, you know, we've talked about the trans women and biological women's sports issue many,

many times. I am It is an 80/20 issue. I am on the 80% side of it. There is a biological advantage, obviously. But this is so much broader than that. And it was interesting that, you know, this comes out right around the same time that there are reports that the Trump administration is going to cut down on loan grants for people pursuing majors that are not going to earn them enough money. Right, so that they get to decide what you're majoring in. Now, if my daughters come to me and they say, you know, I want to go spend $300,000 on a gender studies degree, I might say,

"Okay, look, let's talk about, you know, where you're going with that. What what the prospects are." But the federal government doesn't get to decide those things, especially if they're not even helping people with loan repayments anyway. That would be one thing, right? If you said, "Okay, well, there's $50,000 or $100,000 on the other side of this, let's talk about the decisions that you're making and what majors are leading, you know, to high-paying jobs or at least jobs where you'll be able to pay back your loans." But, that's not this either. It's just always a crusade against what they perceive to be the left or the things that the left are

interested in. And I'm really sick of it. >> Yeah, this is mostly my sense is this is mostly optics, and that is federal courts have already vacated, whether you agree with their decision or not, federal courts have already vacated the Biden rule in January 2025. So, this really just largely formalizes what was already dead. It's It's sort of like announcing the demolition of a building that's already been torn down for a photo op. So, again, this is an attempt to inflame the base and talk about third bathrooms and

you know, transgender women breaking the nose of a 14-year-old girl in a high school volleyball game. And they're doing it now because it seems to be an issue that turns out the base. And 35 days out is when you pull the lever, even if the lever is sort of like totally non-consequential. Um the I mean, I go to where I go to is the following. The education issue no one campaigns on is that men are about 40% of college students, 40 to 60, so 50% more women are in college than men, which has, I think, a lot of knock-on

effects. And meanwhile, both parties are fighting about locker rooms, which basically impacts almost nobody, while boys quietly disappear from classrooms. And in my view, that's the kind of the tidal line crisis that no one no one is no one's talking about or feeling. So, there's just so few issues that are so incendiary that affect so few people and should [snorts] be you know, I go so Republican on this and that is let the school and the parents decide. I can't imagine being on a school board.

I was in a I was on the board of my kids school in a fairly purple / red district. If there was a 14-year-old trans girl who wanted to play volleyball, I can't imagine anyone unless they're really awful would not think that was a good idea or have a problem with it. At the same time, we can have some nuance here. And the International Olympic Committee can put out a statement saying no, you can't compete in women's sports if you were born a female. I I just think there's some logical solutions here to be {quote} left up to

the states and local schools. And then there's the argument of well, what about people who went through transition before testosterone had an impact on them. I mean, we're literally getting down to dozens of people here. And where I think the Democrats have shot themselves in the foot is they're so I don't know. Quite frankly, self-righteous about this topic and go to an area that seems just a little bit crazy that they end up creating an opening for people to get elected who then turn around and demonize this community and kick them out of the military and scrub

their names from ships. This is not I think we've been very smart on this issue. >> Co-signed, Democrats haven't been very smart. Then insert whatever topic. But I just wanted to add that this is about more than trans kids. This is this reaches sexual orientation. >> Yeah. >> Which is everything else in the acronym. So I think that we shouldn't lose sight of this being an expansion of the fight that they were having about trans kids. And yes, they'd

already rescinded the Biden era rule, but as layers get built on top of layers, they become harder to unwind. >> Mhm. >> That's what stuck out to me about it, that it it did seem like this is more expansive than the conversations that we've been having about, you know, Lia Thomas and Riley Gaines, for instance. But I'm in agreement with you. >> That makes sense. Uh so, staying in the education realm, a new lawsuit has put the Cornell 7 back in the spotlight. A former Cornell student alleges she was

drugged and sexually assaulted by seven fraternity members in 2024. Prosecutors initially declined to file charges, but have now reopened the investigation and are seeking a grand jury review. Let's listen to AOC talking about it. >> Their fraternity knew. This was reported to Cornell University. And after looking into this matter, they expelled two of them and made the rest write essays. The culture of rape, sexual assault, and pedophilia

is protected in elite institutions across the United States, and including Cornell University in this instance. This entire country is sick and tired of not just financially corrupt, but morally corrupt leadership in every institution. >> This is a really rough one. I mean, I it almost feels like we shouldn't be talking about it this way. I I mean, we have to talk about it, but, you know, getting in the weeds of, you know, what

the DA says Jane Doe's statement was from 2024, and he's only released a summary of it, you know, and saying that she didn't allege she was drugged without her knowledge or she didn't consent to engage in sexual activities in the 2024 version. That is different than what's going on now. But the play-by-play of the interaction that evening between her and getting up to seven men. It's just the stuff of nightmares, right? You know, even if there was an agreement around having the threesome and another

men man entering and joining in, other men coming in and out, doing drugs off of her body. And I guess my big question is if the district attorney is accepting that that was what happened, right? That was the 2024 story that he got, why wouldn't he have done his own investigation on top of it? Like, wouldn't you think that any normal human being, let alone someone with a job this important, would say, "Um, I actually maybe we should look under the hood a

little bit of what's going on when there's uh one girl and at peak seven guys involved in this?" And I'm not saying that, you know, people can't consent to a threesome or, you know, want to do these things, especially when they're on drugs and enibriated, but I cannot imagine taking her 2024 statement and just thinking, "Oh, you know, this is the end of it." Let alone then when you see what the university does in response to it, you know, barring the fraternity

from campus and two getting thrown out and then the rest having to write essays. And this stuck out to me. There's a 2025 survey conducted uh by Cornell that found that 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing, quote, non-consensual sexual contact during their time at Cornell. 35%? >> Yeah, this is I mean, there's just no getting around it. This is awful. You know, so these are allegations and a grand jury is the right venue. It should have been reopened. They should do a

good job. They should bring in the right people with domain expertise to handle this case. And the data I saw was from the AAU that roughly one in four undergraduate women report non-consensual sexual contact in college. And I mean essentially universities are running a risk no parent would sign off on if you described it in plain English. And one of the things we always talk about as parents that we like about college is we think of it as a safe place. And the reality is this data shows that it is not a safe place for women.

The reality is young men and alcohol in groups and no adult supervision are just an incredibly dangerous combination on any campus not only to other people but to themselves. >> You know, I think the university took this seriously, but they obviously don't want it to be massively in the public eye as this is going on. And I know that what happened at Duke with the lacrosse players, you know, sits with universities. And they you know, think about it the terrible implications for those three players um who were

eventually cleared of all charges. And the reputational damage for the kids and for the university. But I think that it is incumbent upon the universities if they are in fact taking it seriously to make noise about that because it is sending a signal that they understand how important this is and the implications for everybody involved, right? For Jane Doe and for the seven you know, frat guys that were a party to this. And I know that you don't want to

have a a redux of what happened at Duke necessarily. And there are kids that make very poor consensual decisions, right? Where there should be no criminal charges filed. But I think the fact that it was so quiet what was going on and that the DA did not do his own personal investigation using the strength of his office to talk to more people, to do more investigating has created an even bigger problem for

them and they're probably looking back at 2024 full of regret that they hadn't approached it differently. But if you're seeing stats also from 25 to 35% of women that are saying that they are confronted with unwanted, you know, sexual advances during their time in college >> problem >> that's that's way too much, right? Like even if you're controlling for people that might misread a situation or might regret something, you know, I'm not trying to be the your skirt was too short person at all. I'm just saying there are, you

know, there are times where you have a reaction to something and then in hindsight you're like it wasn't what I I thought that it was. >> That's like we're accepting this culture. Like those numbers are that high. >> Yeah, that's almost saying it's been a little bit normalized. >> Yeah. >> So, this is the bottom line, this is a sandwich.
